claim: Numerous cell functions are accompanied by phenotypic changes in viscoelastic properties.
source: Numerous cell functions are accompanied by phenotypic changes in viscoelastic properties, and measuring them can help elucidate higher level cellular functions in health and disease.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the subsequent research presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells are suspended in a high-viscosity fluid and pumped through a 5.8 cm long and 200 µm wide microfluidic channel.
source: Cells are suspended in a high-viscosity fluid and are pumped with high pressure through a 5.8 cm long and 200 µm wide microfluidic channel.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup used in the study.

claim: The fluid shear stress induces large, ellipsoidal cell deformations.
source: The fluid shear stress induces large, ear ellipsoidal cell deformations.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data and shown in figures.

claim: The flow profile in the channel causes cells to rotate in a tank-treading manner.
source: In addition, the flow profile in the channel causes the cells to rotate in a tank-treading manner.
evidence: This is observed experimentally and shown in Video 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Viscoelastic cell properties are extracted based on a theoretical framework developed by R. Roscoe that describes the deformation of a viscoelastic sphere in a viscous fluid under steady laminar flow.
source: From the cell deformation and tank treading frequency, we extract the frequency-dependent viscoelastic cell properties based on a theoretical framework developed by R. Roscoe [1] that describes the deformation of a viscoelastic sphere in a viscous fluid under steady laminar flow.
evidence: The method is based on Roscoe's theoretical framework, which is cited.

claim: The accuracy of the method is confirmed using atomic force microscopy-calibrated polyacrylamide beads and cells.
source: We confirm the accuracy of the method using atomic force microscopy-calibrated polyacrylamide beads and cells.
evidence: Validation experiments are described in the Results section and shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Suspended cells exhibit power-law, soft glassy rheological behavior.
source: Our measurements demonstrate that suspended cells exhibit power-law, soft glassy rheological behavior that is cell-cycle-dependent and mediated by the physical interplay between the actin filament and intermediate filament networks.
evidence: This is demonstrated through measurements shown in Figure 3 and discussed in the Results section.

claim: Cell rheological behavior is cell-cycle-dependent.
source: Our measurements demonstrate that suspended cells exhibit power-law, soft glassy rheological behavior that is cell-cycle-dependent and mediated by the physical interplay between the actin filament and intermediate filament networks.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with Fucci cell cycle indicator experiments.

claim: Cell rheological behavior is mediated by the physical interplay between the actin filament and intermediate filament networks.
source: Our measurements demonstrate that suspended cells exhibit power-law, soft glassy rheological behavior that is cell-cycle-dependent and mediated by the physical interplay between the actin filament and intermediate filament networks.
evidence: This is demonstrated through cytochalasin D treatment experiments on cells with and without intermediate filaments, shown in Figure 7.

claim: The activation of neutrophils in response to pro-inflammatory agents is typically accompanied by a marked increase in cell stiffness.
source: For example, the activation of neutrophils in response to pro-inflammatory agents is typically accompanied by a marked increase in cell stiffness (Frank, 1990; Fabry et al., 2001), which can subsequently lead to a sequestration of the stiffened cells in small capillaries for example of the lung (Doerschuk et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stiffened neutrophils can sequester in small capillaries of the lung.
source: For example, the activation of neutrophils in response to pro-inflammatory agents is typically accompanied by a marked increase in cell stiffness (Frank, 1990; Fabry et al., 2001), which can subsequently lead to a sequestration of the stiffened cells in small capillaries for example of the lung (Doerschuk et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Doerschuk et al., 1993.

claim: Cells are suspended in a high-viscosity medium with viscosity between 0.5–10 Pa s.
source: The cells are suspended in a high-viscosity (0.5–10 Pa s) fluid (e.g. a 2% alginate solution) and are pumped at pressures of typically between 50 and 300 kPa through a several centimeter long microfluidic channel with a square cross section (200x200 µm in our set-up).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: Cells are pumped at pressures typically between 50 and 300 kPa.
source: The cells are suspended in a high-viscosity (0.5–10 Pa s) fluid (e.g. a 2% alginate solution) and are pumped at pressures of typically between 50 and 300 kPa through a several centimeter long microfluidic channel with a square cross section (200x200 µm in our set-up).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: Images are stored and analyzed off-line at a speed of around 50 frames/s on a standard desktop PC equipped with a graphics card.
source: Images are stored and analyzed off-line at a speed of around 50 frames/s on a standard desktop PC equipped with a graphics card.
evidence: This describes the data processing capabilities of the method.

claim: The shear stress profile inside a long microfluidic channel depends only on the pressure gradient along the channel and the channel geometry.
source: The method takes advantage of two physical principles: First, the shear stress profile inside a long microfluidic channel depends only on the pressure gradient along the channel, which can be precisely controlled, and the channel geometry, which is fixed.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of fluid mechanics applied in the method.

claim: The shear stress profile does not depend on the viscosity of the cell suspension medium.
source: Importantly, the shear stress profile does not depend on the viscosity of the cell suspension medium and smoothly increases from zero at the channel center to a maximum value at the channel walls.
evidence: This is a consequence of the fluid mechanics in the channel geometry and is verified experimentally.

claim: Cells appear circular near the channel center and become increasingly elongated near the channel walls.
source: Accordingly, cells appear circular near the channel center and become increasingly elongated near the channel walls.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The width of the channel is significantly larger than the cell diameter.
source: As the width of the channel is significantly larger than the cell diameter, fluid shear stresses remain approximately constant across the cell surface, which considerably simplifies the fluid dynamics computations compared to existing microfluidic methods.
evidence: This is a design feature of the experimental setup.

claim: Fluid shear stresses remain approximately constant across the cell surface.
source: As the width of the channel is significantly larger than the cell diameter, fluid shear stresses remain approximately constant across the cell surface, which considerably simplifies the fluid dynamics computations compared to existing microfluidic methods.
evidence: This is a consequence of the channel geometry and is shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Shear-flow induced tank-treading was first theoretically explored by Einstein in 1906.
source: Shear-flow induced tank-treading was first theoretically explored by Einstein, 1906, and was later experimentally observed by H. Schmid-Schönbein et al. in sheared red blood cell suspensions (Schmid-Schöenbein and Wells, 1969; Fischer et al., 1978).
evidence: This is a historical reference supported by citations.

claim: Tank-treading was experimentally observed by H. Schmid-Schönbein et al. in sheared red blood cell suspensions.
source: Shear-flow induced tank-treading was first theoretically explored by Einstein, 1906, and was later experimentally observed by H. Schmid-Schönbein et al. in sheared red blood cell suspensions (Schmid-Schöenbein and Wells, 1969; Fischer et al., 1978).
evidence: This is a historical reference supported by citations.

claim: Tank-treading arises as the flow speed of the suspension fluid in contact with the cell surface facing the channel center is larger compared to the flow speed at the opposite side.
source: Tank-treading arises as the flow speed of the suspension fluid in contact with the cell surface facing the channel center is larger compared to the flow speed at the opposite side.
evidence: This is an explanation of the physical mechanism of tank-treading.

claim: The rotational speed of tank-treading motion increases with increasing shear rate near the channel walls.
source: Hence, the rotational speed of this tank-treading motion increases with increasing shear rate near the channel walls.
evidence: This is observed experimentally and shown in Figure 2j and k.

claim: Tank-treading in combination with the cell's viscous properties leads to energy dissipation.
source: Tank-treading in combination with the cell's viscous properties leads to energy dissipation, which limits the increase of cell strain at higher stresses near the channel walls.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation that is consistent with the observed data.

claim: Most cells have undergone several full rotations before reaching the field of view.
source: Since the microfluidic channel is several centimeters long, most cells, with the exception of those in the center of the channel, have already undergone several full rotations before reaching the field of view.
evidence: This is inferred from the channel length and flow conditions.

claim: Cell deformations are in a steady state when measured.
source: Therefore, the cell deformations are in a steady state, which is another major difference compared to existing microfluidic approaches and greatly simplifies the calculation of viscoelastic cell parameters.
evidence: This is a consequence of the long channel and is a key feature of the method.

claim: The Roscoe model assumes that cells behave as a Kelvin-Voigt body consisting of an elastic spring in parallel with a resistive dash-pot element.
source: The Roscoe model assumes that cells behave as a Kelvin-Voigt body consisting of an elastic spring in parallel with a resistive (or viscous) dash-pot element.
evidence: This describes the theoretical model used for analysis.

claim: A commonly used simplified assumption is that the elastic and viscous elements of the Kelvin-Voigt body are constant.
source: A commonly used simplified assumption is that the elastic and viscous elements of the Kelvin-Voigt body are constant (Fregin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a reference to a common modeling approach in the literature.

claim: Polyacrylamide beads are used to verify the accuracy of the method.
source: Using cell lines and calibrated polyacrylamide beads, we verify that our method provides accurate quantitative measurements of viscoelastic properties.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: Measurement results are not or only marginally influenced by the viscosity of the suspension fluid.
source: Measurement results are not or only marginally influenced by experimental details such as the viscosity of the suspension fluid or the time point after suspending the cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3f and g.

claim: Measurement results are not or only marginally influenced by the time point after suspending the cells.
source: Measurement results are not or only marginally influenced by experimental details such as the viscosity of the suspension fluid or the time point after suspending the cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3h and i.

claim: The cell's viscoelastic properties conform to soft glassy power-law rheology.
source: We demonstrate that the cell's viscoelastic properties measured with our method conform to soft glassy power-law rheology that has been reported for a wide range of cells measured with different methods.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3a and b and discussed in the Results section.

claim: The method can be used for dose-response measurements of drugs that induce actin cytoskeleton disassembly.
source: We also show that our method can be used for dose-response measurements of drugs that induce actin cytoskeleton disassembly, and that these responses are modulated by the cell cycle and the intermediate filament network of the cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Drug responses are modulated by the cell cycle.
source: We also show that our method can be used for dose-response measurements of drugs that induce actin cytoskeleton disassembly, and that these responses are modulated by the cell cycle and the intermediate filament network of the cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8.

claim: Drug responses are modulated by the intermediate filament network of the cells.
source: We also show that our method can be used for dose-response measurements of drugs that induce actin cytoskeleton disassembly, and that these responses are modulated by the cell cycle and the intermediate filament network of the cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: A neural network detects cells that are in focus at the mid-plane of the microchannel.
source: Using a neural network, we detect cells that are in focus at the mid-plane of the microchannel (Figure 1b), and segment their shapes (Figure 1d).
evidence: This describes the image analysis method used.

claim: The slope of the strain versus stress relationship decreases for higher stress values.
source: In particular, the slope of the strain versus stress relationship decreases for higher stress values.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2c.

claim: The decrease in slope at higher stress is predominantly due to a dissipative process caused by the tank tread-like motion of the cells.
source: This behavior is predominantly due to a dissipative process caused by the tank tread-like motion of the cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the theoretical model.

claim: The tank-treading frequency of a cell is zero at the channel center and increases towards the channel walls.
source: We find that the tank-treading frequency of a cell is zero at the channel center and increases towards the channel walls (Figure 2j and k).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2j and k.

claim: Tank-treading dissipates energy in proportion to the cell's internal viscosity, rotation frequency, and strain.
source: Tank-treading dissipates energy in proportion to the cell's internal viscosity, rotation frequency, and strain.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the Roscoe model.

claim: Energy dissipation limits the cell strain in regions of high shear rate and shear stress.
source: This energy dissipation therefore limits the cell strain in regions of high shear rate and hence shear stress (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: With increasing loss modulus, cells deform less but align more in flow direction.
source: With increasing loss modulus, cells are also predicted to deform less but to align more in flow direction.
evidence: This is a prediction from the Roscoe theory.

claim: There is an inverse relationship between stiffness and fluidity, whereby stiffer cells tend to be less fluid-like.
source: Moreover, also in agreement with previous reports, we find an inverse relationship between stiffness and fluidity, whereby stiffer cells tend to be less fluid-like (Fabry et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2005; Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: Cell fluidity remains constant over the pressure range from 100 kPa to 300 kPa.
source: Cell fluidity remains constant over this pressure range, but the median stiffness of the cell population increases with increasing pressure by 33% (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3d and e.

claim: The median stiffness of the cell population increases with increasing pressure by 33%.
source: Cell fluidity remains constant over this pressure range, but the median stiffness of the cell population increases with increasing pressure by 33% (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Increasing alginate concentration leads to a slight but not statistically significant increase in stiffness and fluidity.
source: This causes the shear rate to decrease and leads to a slight but not statistically significant increase in stiffness and fluidity (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3f and g.

claim: The increase of cell stiffness at a higher driving pressure is induced by stress-stiffening and not by a higher shear rate.
source: Hence, the increase of cell stiffness at a higher driving pressure is induced by stress-stiffening and not by a higher shear rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments varying pressure and alginate concentration.

claim: Cell stiffness and fluidity remain stable over a period of up to 60 min after suspending the cells in a 2% alginate solution.
source: We also verify that cell stiffness and fluidity remain stable over a period of up to 60 min after suspending the cells in a 2% alginate solution (Figure 3g and h).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3h and i.

claim: Fluidity increases slightly at higher strains for polyacrylamide beads, likely due to fluid-induced (poroelastic) relaxation processes.
source: Fluidity increases slightly at higher strains (Figure 4f), likely due to fluid-induced (poroelastic) relaxation processes (Kalcioglu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4f and is attributed to poroelastic effects based on a citation.

claim: NIH-3T3 fibroblasts soften with increasing doses of latrunculin B according to a sigmoidal (Hill-Langmuir) relationship.
source: NIH-3T3 fibroblasts soften with increasing doses of LatB (1–1000 nM) according to a sigmoidal (Hill-Langmuir) relationship, with a maximum response of 1.47-fold and a half-maximum dose of EC50=35.2 nM (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The latrunculin B dose-response for NIH-3T3 cells has a maximum response of 1.47-fold and EC50=35.2 nM.
source: NIH-3T3 fibroblasts soften with increasing doses of LatB (1–1000 nM) according to a sigmoidal (Hill-Langmuir) relationship, with a maximum response of 1.47-fold and a half-maximum dose of EC50=35.2 nM (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The latrunculin B dose-response for NIH-3T3 cells agrees with published data obtained using real-time deformability cytometry on HL-60 cells.
source: These responses agree with published data obtained using real-time deformability cytometry (RT-DC) measurements on HL-60 cells (maximum response 1.46-fold, EC50=26.5 nM) (Urbanska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with published data.

claim: HL-60 cells measured with shear flow cytometry have an EC50 similar to published data (26.4 nM) but a much higher maximum response (5.0-fold).
source: When we measure pro-myoblast HL-60 suspension cells with our setup, EC50 is similar to published data (26.4 nM), but the maximum response is much higher (5.0-fold) (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b.

claim: NIH-3T3 cells express high levels of the intermediate filament protein vimentin.
source: To explore the attenuated LatB responsiveness of NIH-3T3 fibroblasts compared to HL-60 leukemia cells, we reasoned that NIH-3T3 cells express high levels of the intermediate filament protein vimentin (Figure 7a) that may protect the cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Vimentin may protect cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized.
source: To explore the attenuated LatB responsiveness of NIH-3T3 fibroblasts compared to HL-60 leukemia cells, we reasoned that NIH-3T3 cells express high levels of the intermediate filament protein vimentin (Figure 7a) that may protect the cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Cytochalasin D binds to the barbed end of filamentous actin and leads to a net depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: To test this idea, we measure the stiffness of NIH-3T3 and vimentin-knock-out (vim(-/-)) fibroblasts in response to 30 min treatment with cytochalasin D (2 µM), which binds to the barbed end of filamentous actin and—similar to LatB—leads to a net depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a known mechanism of cytochalasin D action.

claim: Cytochalasin D treated vim(-/-) cells soften by a considerably greater extent (2.16-fold) compared to wild-type cells (1.22 fold).
source: We find that cytochalasin D treated vim(-/-) cells soften by a considerably greater extent (2.16-fold) compared to wild-type cells (1.22 fold) (Figure 7b and c), in support of the notion that vimentin stabilizes the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b and c.

claim: Vimentin stabilizes the cytoskeleton.
source: We find that cytochalasin D treated vim(-/-) cells soften by a considerably greater extent (2.16-fold) compared to wild-type cells (1.22 fold) (Figure 7b and c), in support of the notion that vimentin stabilizes the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Desmin is the dominant intermediate filament in skeletal muscle.
source: Desmin, which is the dominant intermediate filament in skeletal muscle, forms an intermediate filament network in fibroblasts that is structurally similar to the vimentin network in wild-type cells (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about desmin.

claim: Desmin forms an intermediate filament network in fibroblasts that is structurally similar to the vimentin network in wild-type cells.
source: Desmin, which is the dominant intermediate filament in skeletal muscle, forms an intermediate filament network in fibroblasts that is structurally similar to the vimentin network in wild-type cells (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Vim(-/-) desmin-expressing MEFs display an attenuated cytochalasin D response (1.37-fold).
source: Similar to vimentin-expressing MEFs, vim(-/-) desmin-expressing MEFs also display an attenuated cytochalasin D response (1.37-fold), confirming that both the vimentin and desmin intermediate filament network can protect cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Both the vimentin and desmin intermediate filament network can protect cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized.
source: Similar to vimentin-expressing MEFs, vim(-/-) desmin-expressing MEFs also display an attenuated cytochalasin D response (1.37-fold), confirming that both the vimentin and desmin intermediate filament network can protect cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Larger NIH-3T3 cells tend to be softer compared to smaller cells.
source: In our measurements, we observe that larger NIH-3T3 cells tend to be softer compared to smaller cells (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The size-dependence of cell stiffness might be attributable to cell cycle progression.
source: We hypothesized that this weak size-dependence of cell stiffness might be attributable to cell cycle progression, which leads to changes in chromatin compaction and cell volume.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Cell cycle progression leads to changes in chromatin compaction and cell volume.
source: We hypothesized that this weak size-dependence of cell stiffness might be attributable to cell cycle progression, which leads to changes in chromatin compaction and cell volume.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle progression.

claim: Cell radius increases with cell cycle progression.
source: We find as expected that cell radius increases with cell cycle progression (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Cell stiffness steadily increases towards the end of the G1 and the beginning of the S-phase.
source: In addition, cell stiffness steadily increases towards the end of the G1 and the beginning of the S-phase, and then rapidly decreases as the cell cycle progresses (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8e.

claim: Cell stiffness rapidly decreases as the cell cycle progresses after the beginning of S-phase.
source: In addition, cell stiffness steadily increases towards the end of the G1 and the beginning of the S-phase, and then rapidly decreases as the cell cycle progresses (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8e.

claim: Changes in cell stiffness and cell radius occur at different stages of the cell cycle.
source: When we bin the cells according to their green fluorescent intensities (i.e. according to their cell cycle progression) and plot stiffness versus cell radius (Figure 8f), we find substantially larger and non-monotonic fluctuations of cell stiffness versus cell radius, compared to the smaller, monotonic decrease of cell stiffness in the radius-binned data (Figure 8c). These differences arise because changes in cell stiffness and cell radius occur at different stages of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Established methods such as atomic force microscopy, micropipette aspirations, or magnetic tweezer microrheology have a relatively low throughput of typically below 10–100 cells/hr.
source: Viscoelastic cell properties can be measured with established methods such as atomic force microscopy (Cordes et al., 2020), micropipette aspirations (Zhelev et al., 1994), or magnetic tweezer microrheology (Bonakdar et al., 2016). These methods have a relatively low throughput of typically below 10–100 cells/hr.
evidence: This is a comparison with existing methods based on citations.

claim: The need to measure cell mechanical properties with substantially higher throughput led to the recent development of various microfluidic techniques.
source: The need to measure cell mechanical properties with substantially higher throughput led to the recent development of various microfluidic techniques (Urbanska et al., 2020) including hydrodynamic stretching (Gossett et al., 2012), real-time deformability cytometry (Otto et al., 2015; Fregin et al., 2019), micro-filtration (Rowat et al., 2012), and micro-constriction systems (Lange et al., 2015; Lange et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a review of the field based on citations.

claim: The method uses a simple microfluidic channel with one inlet and outlet, without a flow-focussing geometry.
source: We suspend cells in a medium that is pumped with high pressure (typically 50–300 kPa) through a long, parallel microfluidic channel with one inlet and outlet (no flow-focussing geometry is needed).
evidence: This describes a design feature of the method.

claim: Simple microfluidic channels are commercially available at low cost.
source: Such simple microfluidic channels are commercially available at low cost, which we expect will facilitate a widespread adoption of the technique.
evidence: This is a practical consideration about the method.

claim: The large driving pressure gives rise to sufficiently large (>50 Pa) shear stresses to induce measurable cell deformations.
source: The large driving pressure gives rise to sufficiently large (>50 Pa) shear stresses to induce measurable cell deformations.
evidence: This is a design feature of the method.

claim: The high pressure can be controlled with a simple pressure regulator, without the need for a precise microfluidic controller.
source: The high pressure can be controlled with a simple pressure regulator, without the need for a precise microfluidic controller—another advantage compared to existing methods that typically operate under lower pressure.
evidence: This is a practical advantage of the method.

claim: The large channel diameter prevents clogging due to debris.
source: The width and height of the channel (200 µm) are much larger than the cell diameter, which prevents clogging due to debris that is often encountered in microfluidic constriction-based systems (Lange et al., 2015; Lange et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a practical advantage of the method.

claim: The large channel diameter ensures that fluid shear stresses do not vary appreciably across the cell.
source: Most importantly, the large channel diameter ensures that fluid shear stresses do not vary appreciably across the cell, which simplifies the analysis of cell mechanical properties as the cells do not deform into complex bullet- or hourglass-like shapes as seen in other methods (Lange et al., 2015; Lange et al., 2017; Urbanska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a design feature that simplifies analysis.

claim: Suspending cells in a fluid with high viscosity achieves a flow speed that is sufficiently low to capture cells without motion blur at a typical exposure time of 30 µs.
source: By suspending the cells in a fluid with high viscosity (typically >1 Pa⋅s), we achieve a flow speed that is sufficiently low (<20 mm/s) so that the cells' speed, position, and shape can be captured without motion blur at a typical exposure time of 30 µs using a standard CMOS-camera mounted to a routine laboratory microscope.
evidence: This is a design feature of the method.

claim: The lateral flow profile in the channel causes a tank-treading-like cell motion, which imposes periodic cell deformations with frequencies on the order of 10 Hz.
source: The lateral flow profile in the channel causes a tank-treading-like cell motion, which imposes periodic cell deformations with frequencies on the order of 10 Hz.
evidence: This is observed experimentally.

claim: At low frequencies and strain rates around 10 Hz, elastic cell properties dominate over viscous cell properties.
source: At such low frequencies and strain rates, elastic cell properties dominate over viscous cell properties (Fabry et al., 2001; Mietke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: The cell transit through the microfluidic channel lasts for several seconds.
source: The cell transit through the microfluidic channel lasts for several seconds, which is much longer than the period time of the cells' tank treading rotation, implying that the measured cell deformations can safely be assumed to have reached a steady-state.
evidence: This is inferred from the channel length and flow speed.

claim: Measuring visco-elastic parameters from steady-state cell deformations has a major advantage over existing microfluidic techniques in that no visco-elastic models or pre-conceived response functions are needed.
source: Measuring visco-elastic parameters from steady-state cell deformations has a major advantage over existing microfluidic techniques in that no visco-elastic models (e.g. Maxwell, Voigt etc.) or pre-conceived response functions (e.g. exponential, bi-exponential, power-law etc.) are needed to fit the transient cell deformation responses during the cells' passage through narrow constrictions and channels (Lange et al., 2015; Fregin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological advantage compared to other techniques.

claim: If an exponential function is fitted to a power-law creep response, the resulting viscoelastic cell properties would largely depend on the time scale of the experiment.
source: If for example an exponential function is fitted to a power-law creep response, the resulting viscoelastic cell properties would largely depend on the time scale of the experiment (e.g. the passage time of the cell through the microfluidic constriction or channel) and less so on the cell's intrinsic mechanical properties (Fabry et al., 2001; Lange et al., 2015; Fregin et al., 2019)
evidence: This is a critique of other methods based on citations.

claim: The values obtained with the shear flow method are not influenced by the time scale of the experiment.
source: By contrast, the values obtained with our method are not influenced by the time scale of the experiment.
evidence: This is an advantage of the steady-state measurement approach.

claim: Once the flow velocity profile is known, viscoelastic properties can be determined from a single image because all cell deformations are in a steady-state.
source: Hence, once the flow velocity profile is known, we can determine the viscoelastic properties from a single image because all cell deformations are in a steady-state.
evidence: This is a consequence of the steady-state measurement approach.

claim: User-friendly software for image acquisition and data analysis is provided and can be downloaded at https://github.com/fabrylab/shear_flow_deformation_cytometer.
source: We provide user-friendly software for image acquisition and data analysis on a standard PC, which can be downloaded at https://github.com/fabrylab/shear_flow_deformation_cytometer (copy archived at swh:1:rev:2d35a697243c432cddd52e10d2e3c5121f922adf; Gerum, 2022).
evidence: This is information about software availability.

claim: The method stores acquired uncompressed images on a hard drive, which amounts to nearly 4 GB for typically 10,000 images.
source: Currently, the method stores the acquired uncompressed images on a hard drive, which in the case of typically 10,000 images for a single experiment lasting 20 s amounts to a storage space of nearly 4 GB.
evidence: This describes a current limitation of the method.

claim: Image data are analyzed afterwards at a rate of around 50 images per second, which can take several minutes.
source: The image data are analyzed afterwards, which at a rate of around 50 images per second can take several minutes.
evidence: This describes the current data processing speed.

claim: The computation of viscoelastic properties is based on a theoretical model proposed by R. Roscoe that describes the deformation of homogeneous, isotropic, incompressible neo-Hookean viscoelastic spherical particles under fluid shear stress.
source: The computation of viscoelastic properties is based on a theoretical model proposed by R. Roscoe that describes the deformation of homogeneous, isotropic, incompressible neo-Hookean viscoelastic spherical particles under fluid shear stress (Roscoe, 1967).
evidence: This describes the theoretical basis of the method.

claim: Cells in suspensions are known to deform non-linearly with stress- or strain stiffening.
source: Cells in suspensions, however, are known to deform non-linearly (Lange et al., 2017), with stress- or strain stiffening that is more pronounced than the stiffening predicted for a neo-Hookean material.
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claim: The measurements represent an effective secant modulus and not a small-strain tangential modulus.
source: Therefore, our measurements represent an effective secant modulus and not a small-strain tangential modulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the measurements represent.

claim: Cells do not consist of a homogeneous material but of different components with different mechanical properties.
source: Moreover, cells do not consist of a homogeneous material but of different components (e.g. the cell cortex and the nucleus) with different mechanical properties (Zhelev et al., 1994; Rowat et al., 2012; Mietke et al., 2015; Cordes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: Cells do not always deform into ellipsoidal shapes but occasionally deform into sigmoidal shapes.
source: As a consequence, cells do not always deform into ellipsoidal shapes but occasionally deform into sigmoidal shapes, which becomes more pronounced in response to larger shear stresses or drugs that soften the cytoskeleton, such as cytochalasin D or latrunculin B.
evidence: This is observed in the experiments.

claim: Cell rheological measurements agree with previously published findings that suspended cells show behavior consistent with power-law rheology.
source: Despite the simplified assumptions of the Roscoe theory, however, our cell rheological measurements agree with previously published findings that were obtained using a range of different methods and models, namely that suspended cells show a behavior that is consistent with power-law rheology, that the elasticity of individual cells is log-normal distributed, that the fluidity of individual cells is normal-distributed, and that stiffness and fluidity scale inversely (Fabry et al., 2001; Alcaraz et al., 2003; Desprat et al., 2005; Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: The elasticity of individual cells is log-normal distributed.
source: Despite the simplified assumptions of the Roscoe theory, however, our cell rheological measurements agree with previously published findings that were obtained using a range of different methods and models, namely that suspended cells show a behavior that is consistent with power-law rheology, that the elasticity of individual cells is log-normal distributed, that the fluidity of individual cells is normal-distributed, and that stiffness and fluidity scale inversely (Fabry et al., 2001; Alcaraz et al., 2003; Desprat et al., 2005; Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: The fluidity of individual cells is normal-distributed.
source: Despite the simplified assumptions of the Roscoe theory, however, our cell rheological measurements agree with previously published findings that were obtained using a range of different methods and models, namely that suspended cells show a behavior that is consistent with power-law rheology, that the elasticity of individual cells is log-normal distributed, that the fluidity of individual cells is normal-distributed, and that stiffness and fluidity scale inversely (Fabry et al., 2001; Alcaraz et al., 2003; Desprat et al., 2005; Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: Stiffness and fluidity scale inversely.
source: Despite the simplified assumptions of the Roscoe theory, however, our cell rheological measurements agree with previously published findings that were obtained using a range of different methods and models, namely that suspended cells show a behavior that is consistent with power-law rheology, that the elasticity of individual cells is log-normal distributed, that the fluidity of individual cells is normal-distributed, and that stiffness and fluidity scale inversely (Fabry et al., 2001; Alcaraz et al., 2003; Desprat et al., 2005; Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: Experimental findings are in agreement with predictions from soft glassy rheology.
source: These experimental findings are in agreement with predictions from soft glassy rheology (Sollich, 1998; Fabry et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison with theoretical predictions.

claim: Measurements are insensitive to changes in the viscosity of the suspension medium.
source: Our measurements are insensitive to changes in the viscosity of the suspension medium, demonstrating that the fluid-mechanical assumptions of the Roscoe theory hold in the case of living cells in a shear-thinning suspension fluid.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3f and g.

claim: Cells appear stiffer when measured at higher driving pressures, likely due to stress- or strain-stiffening.
source: We find that cells appear stiffer when measured at higher driving pressures, likely due to stress- or strain-stiffening of the cells (Lange et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3d and is attributed to stress-stiffening.

claim: Polyacrylamide beads show a constant, pressure-independent shear modulus over a 10-fold pressure range.
source: When we measure linearly elastic polyacrylamide beads over a 10-fold pressure range (from 20 to 200 kPa), we see a constant, pressure-independent shear modulus and agreement with the stiffness and fluidity values measured using AFM, demonstrating that the Roscoe theory gives quantitatively accurate estimates, regardless of driving pressure and suspension fluid viscosity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The Roscoe theory gives quantitatively accurate estimates, regardless of driving pressure and suspension fluid viscosity.
source: When we measure linearly elastic polyacrylamide beads over a 10-fold pressure range (from 20 to 200 kPa), we see a constant, pressure-independent shear modulus and agreement with the stiffness and fluidity values measured using AFM, demonstrating that the Roscoe theory gives quantitatively accurate estimates, regardless of driving pressure and suspension fluid viscosity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polyacrylamide bead validation experiments.

claim: Roscoe theory estimates the cell viscosity relative to the viscosity of the suspension fluid.
source: Roscoe theory estimates the cell viscosity relative to the viscosity of the suspension fluid, which for a shear thinning fluid such as alginate can be difficult to measure.
evidence: This is a feature of the Roscoe theory.

claim: The rheological properties of the suspension fluid can be estimated from the fluid profile in the microfluidic channel.
source: However, since we know the fluid profile in the microfluidic channel (from the flow speed of hundreds of cells), we can estimate the rheological properties of the suspension fluid, including its shear thinning behavior.
evidence: This is a capability of the method.

claim: The method measures the complex rheology of the suspension fluid at the same time and under the same conditions as the cells.
source: Moreover, we measure the complex rheology of the suspension fluid at the very same time and under the same conditions (temperature, range of shear rates) as the cells.
evidence: This is an advantage of the method.

claim: The quantification of visco-elastic cell properties does not rely on separate measurements using cone-plate or other types of rheometers.
source: Therefore, unlike other microfluidic cytometry methods (Otto et al., 2015; Fregin et al., 2019), our quantification of visco-elastic cell properties does not rely on separate measurements using cone-plate or other types of rheometers.
evidence: This is an advantage compared to other methods.

claim: The rheological parameters of alginate solutions measured with the shear flow method closely agree with cone-plate rheometer measurements.
source: The rheological parameters of alginate solutions measured with our method closely agree with cone-plate rheometer measurements, with relative deviations of 31% over a shear rate spanning 5 orders in magnitude (from 0.01 to 1000 s-1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The method measures each cell at a single tank-treading frequency that depends on the cell's lateral position in the channel.
source: Our method measures each cell at a single tank-treading frequency that depends on the cell's lateral position in the channel.
evidence: This is a feature of the method.

claim: The method samples the frequency-dependent mechanical properties of a cell population by observing cells at different channel positions.
source: Thus, with our method we sample the frequency-dependent mechanical properties of a cell population simply by observing cells at different channel positions.
evidence: This is a feature of the method.

claim: With existing methods, time- or frequency-dependent cell responses can only be explored by choosing different strain rates.
source: By contrast, with existing methods, time- or frequency-dependent cell responses can only be explored by choosing different strain rates, for example via adjusting the driving pressure (Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with other methods based on a citation.

claim: The tank-treading frequency can be directly measured using particle flow analysis methods in a subset of cells that show small features with high contrast.
source: The tank-treading frequency can be directly measured using particle flow analysis methods in a subset of the cells that shows small features with high contrast (Fischer et al., 1978).
evidence: This describes a measurement approach.

claim: For cells where tank-treading frequency cannot be directly measured, it can be estimated from the local shear rate according to an empirical equation.
source: For the remaining cells, it is possible to estimate the tank treading frequency from the local shear rate according to an empirical equation (Equation 20).
evidence: This describes an estimation approach.

claim: The empirical equation for tank-treading frequency holds for the cell types and suspension fluids used in the study, but may not hold universally for other cell types or suspension fluids.
source: This equation holds for the cell types and suspension fluids used in our study, but we do not claim that it holds universally for other cell types or suspension fluids.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The method shows a considerably larger softening of HL-60 cells (5.4-fold) in response to latrunculin B compared to other microfluidic techniques (1.5-fold).
source: We find in agreement with previous observations a half-maximum dose (EC50) of around 30 nM, but a considerably larger softening of the cells by a factor of 5.4-fold at the highest dose of 1 µM, compared to a softening of only 1.5 fold that is seen with other microfluidic techniques constriction microfluidic constriction-based deformability cytometry (cDC), and real-time deformability cytometry (RT-DC) (Urbanska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6b and compared to published data.

claim: At high strain rates (~100 s⁻¹), viscous cell behavior starts to dominate over cytoskeleton-associated elastic behavior.
source: At these high strain rates, viscous cell behavior starts to dominate over cytoskeleton-associated elastic behavior (Fabry et al., 2001; Mietke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: When cells are measured with extensional flow deformability at strain rates in the kHz-range, they do not appreciably soften in response to latrunculin B.
source: Accordingly, when cells are measured with extensional flow deformability, a method that operates at even higher strain rates in the kHz-range, they do not appreciably soften in response to LatB (Urbanska et al., 2020; Gossett et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claim: The cell softening induced by cytochalasin D is attenuated in the presence of intermediate filaments and becomes more pronounced when intermediate filaments are absent.
source: We also demonstrate that the cell softening induced by cytochalasin D, another actin-depolymerizing drug, is attenuated in the presence of intermediate filaments (vimentin or desmin), and becomes more pronounced when intermediate filaments are absent.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: This finding is in line with earlier reports that intermediate filaments protect cells against excessive strain.
source: This finding is in line with earlier reports that intermediate filaments protect cells against excessive strain (Patteson et al., 2020), and that the absence of vimentin in fibroblasts leaves the cells vulnerable to mechanical stress (Eckes et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: A physical interaction between vimentin intermediate filaments and F-actin bundles as mediated by plectin has been demonstrated by high resolution immuno-electron microscopic methods.
source: A physical interaction between vimentin intermediate filaments and F-actin bundles as mediated by plectin has been demonstrated by high resolution immuno-electron microscopic methods (Svitkina et al., 1996).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claim: The importance of vimentin-actin interactions has been corroborated by high resolution structured illumination microscopy in combination with cryo-electron tomography.
source: The importance of vimentin-actin interactions has furthermore been corroborated by high resolution structured illumination microscopy in combination with cryo-electron tomography, revealing the intimate association and functional crosstalk between vimentin intermediate filaments and F-actin stress fibers (Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claim: The stable introduction of a cytoplasmic intermediate filament protein into intermediate filament-free cells restores their cytoskeletal functionality and mechanical stability.
source: Here, we have directly demonstrated that the stable introduction of a cytoplasmic intermediate filament protein into intermediate filament-free cells restores their cytoskeletal functionality and mechanical stability.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: Shear stress deformability cytometry can be combined with fluorescent imaging.
source: Shear stress deformability cytometry can be combined with fluorescent imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated with Fucci cell cycle indicator experiments.

claim: NIH-3T3 cells stiffen during the course of cell cycle progression in G1 phase, with a maximum stiffness during late G1 – early S-phase.
source: Our data demonstrate that NH-3T3 cells stiffen during the course of cell cycle progression in G1 phase, with a maximum stiffness during late G1 – early S-phase, and then soften before they enter the G2 and M-Phase.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8e.

claim: NIH-3T3 cells soften before they enter the G2 and M-Phase.
source: Our data demonstrate that NH-3T3 cells stiffen during the course of cell cycle progression in G1 phase, with a maximum stiffness during late G1 – early S-phase, and then soften before they enter the G2 and M-Phase.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8e.

claim: Cell volume increases during the transition from G1 to S phase.
source: Since cell volume also increases during the transition from G1 to S phase, we find a slight overall dependence of cell stiffness on cell size in the case of NIH-3T3 cells (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Cell size dependence of stiffness is also detectable in HL-60 and THP1-cells.
source: This cell size dependence is also detectable in HL-60 and THP1-cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Shear flow deformation cytometry provides accurate quantitative measurements of elastic and dissipative cell properties at high throughput.
source: In summary, shear flow deformation cytometry provides accurate quantitative measurements of elastic and dissipative cell properties at high throughput.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The method can be easily and inexpensively implemented on standard or research grade microscopes.
source: The method can be easily and inexpensively implemented on standard or research grade microscopes.
evidence: This is a practical advantage of the method.

claim: Unlike other high-throughput microfluidic methods, the cells are measured under near steady-state conditions at low to moderate strain rates where elastic responses dominate over viscous responses.
source: Unlike other high-throughput microfluidic methods, the cells are measured under near steady-state conditions at low to moderate strain rates where elastic responses dominate over viscous responses.
evidence: This is a key distinguishing feature of the method.
